lesson.title: Arctan: Taming Infinity with a Bounded Slope
lesson.summary: The derivative of arctan x is 1/(1+x^2), a formula with no domain restrictions and no absolute values, making it one of the cleanest results among all the inverse trig derivatives.
lesson.body:
Sine and cosine needed their domains chopped down to a single monotonic piece before they could be inverted; tangent needs the same treatment, but with a twist. Restricting tangent to the open interval (-pi/2, pi/2), it climbs from negative infinity to positive infinity, passing through every real number exactly once. That means arctan x, unlike arcsin or arccos, has domain all real numbers, with range (-pi/2, pi/2) and horizontal asymptotes at y = pi/2 and y = -pi/2.

To differentiate, let y = arctan x, so tan y = x. Differentiating implicitly, sec^2 y times y' = 1, so y' = 1/sec^2 y. The Pythagorean identity sec^2 y = 1 + tan^2 y turns tan y back into x, giving sec^2 y = 1 + x^2. Therefore d/dx[arctan x] = 1/(1+x^2). Notice there is no sign ambiguity to sort out here, unlike the arcsec and arccsc cases coming up next: sec^2 y is always positive, so no absolute value or case split is ever needed.

As practice, differentiate y = arctan(x^3). With u = x^3 and u' = 3x^2, the chain rule gives dy/dx = u'/(1+u^2) = 3x^2/(1+x^6). Checking at x = 0, the slope is 0, which makes sense: near the origin x^3 is far flatter than x itself, so the composite function starts out essentially flat before the arctan curve's usual behavior takes over.

This formula earns its keep constantly in integral calculus, since 1/(1+x^2) integrates right back to arctan x, and it shows up whenever a bounded angle needs to be recovered from an unbounded ratio, such as converting a slope into an angle in a related rates problem.
